correctness.rationale: The Fano evaluations have rank seven: the pure coefficients are set by the three coordinate points, each pair of mixed two-variable terms gives a further independent condition at the corresponding coordinate sum, and the all-ones point sets the XYZ coefficient. The gradient equations of the resulting net have the unique solution [√b:√c:√a]: their matrix on coordinate squares has rank two (there is a nonzero 2-by-2 minor using the square of any nonzero coefficient); Euler's identity gives membership in the cubic. A geometric line not defined over F₂ meets at most one base point, so its residual conic contains at least six, including a full Fano line; Bézout forces an F₂-line factor. Restricting to each of the seven Fano lines gives the seven binary parameter lines. They intersect only in the seven binary points with triple incidence, leaving q−2 points unique to each line and (q−2)(q−4) off them. In the one-factor case a split residual would need another binary line to cover the four off-line base points; the smooth residual is tangent at the unique rational singular point. With no line factor the cubic is geometrically integral and has a repeated tangent line: expansion at the singularity has a square quadratic term, which is nonzero since multiplicity three would force geometric splitting. In coordinates with cusp [0:0:1] and tangent y=0 the model is Zy² plus a binary cubic with nonzero x³ term (otherwise y divides it). Projection from the cusp is birational, and only the tangent direction lies over the cusp, proving the bijection of rational points with the normalization P¹. The two reducible point counts follow by their rational intersections. For the orbit step I checked distinctness and stabilizers directly: off the arrangement the singular-point coordinates are an F₂-basis of a 3-dimensional F₂-subspace W of F_q. A projective stabilizer corresponds bijectively to a nonzero scalar λ with λW=W via its action on that basis. The multipliers preserving W, with zero included, form a subfield and their degree over F₂ divides three. If it is three, W is a scaled F₈, and all such ordered bases are a single orbit, with stabilizer seven and size 24; this exists iff 3 divides m. Otherwise the stabilizer is trivial. Uniqueness of the singular point gives equivariance under G, so the count is for the cubic equations. Independent direct point counts for all forms over q=2,4,8,16 and multiplier checks agree.
residual_risks: Finite field enumeration only corroborates the all-extension argument. Orbits classify equations under the marked Fano-plane group, not abstract curve types or equivalence under PGL₃(F_q).

evidence: The Singer eigenpoints over F₈ and generic cuspidality are prior facts. The finite-extension theorem uses the exact reducibility arrangement, its relation to the unique singular point, and the exclusion of every additional nontrivial stabilizer via subfield multipliers.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The exceptional eigenpoints themselves should not be claimed new. Knowing their existence and the generic cubic type does not provide the curve point-spectrum census or identify precisely which cubic parameters they represent and show no further exceptions. The supported distinction is the combined arithmetic classification, not the underlying Singer calculation in isolation.

value.rationale: The fixed Fano seven-point net is an intrinsic interpolation object and extensions are its natural arithmetic base changes. The result resolves its full finite-field type and point-count distribution, then explains exactly when a nonfree marked-plane symmetry occurs in the cuspidal locus. The simultaneous arithmetic classification is useful even where the underlying line and Singer geometry is standard; it is not a new result about the existence of unexpected cubics alone.
residual_risks: No claim about coarse moduli up to the full projective group over an extension or about extensions beyond characteristic two.
